newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel mulls taxing unemployment benefit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel mulls taxing unemployment benefit.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday he was considering taxing unemployment benefit as part of a planned tax reform due to start in 1999.
Taxing wage replacement benefits was "sensible" in a tax system, Waigel said according to the text of a speech due to be delivered to a conference on tax policy in Munich.
Waigel said basic tax allowances as well as allowances for children and other factors would ensure that such benefits would remain largely exempt from tax in normal circumstances.

Under a broad tax reform which Chancellor Helmut Kohl wants to launch in 1999, top tax rates are to drop from 53 percent to around 35 percent while lowest rates should fall from 25.9 percent to under 20 percent.
Many of the myriad exemptions in Germany's confusing tax laws are to be cut out to help expand the tax base and make up for the revenue shortfall, estimated at 30 billion marks.
But Waigel said the reform would probably not "finance itself fully." It would, however, pay off by boosting economic growth and employment, he said.
The tax committee of the ruling Bonn coalition would present its proposals for the reforms in mid-December, Waigel said.
The reforms would have a gross volume of up to 90 billion marks and would ease the burden on taxpayers by a net 30 billion marks, Waigel said.
The "decisive battleground" in implementing the reform would be the removal of tax breaks, he added.
In addition to taxing unemployment benefit, the government was also considering broader taxation of capital gains and changes in mileage allowance, Waigel said.
He also defended the abolition of wealth tax from the start of 1997, a move fought by the opposition Social Democrats. Removing the tax would save 600 million marks in administrative costs, he said.
